explanation:
## What `decode` is doing

The three fields are contiguous bit ranges, counted from the bottom:

| field | width | how to get it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| offset | `log2(blockBytes)` | `addr & ((1 << offsetBits) - 1)` |
| index | `log2(sets)` | `(addr >> offsetBits) & ((1 << indexBits) - 1)` |
| tag | everything above | `addr >> (offsetBits + indexBits)` |

Check it on `0x1234` with four sets of sixteen bytes: `offsetBits = 4`,
`indexBits = 2`. The offset is `0x1234 & 0xf = 4`. The index is
`(0x1234 >> 4) & 3 = 0x123 & 3 = 3`. The tag is `0x1234 >> 6 = 0x48`.

## The two degenerate geometries

Both are in the tests on purpose, because both are easy to get wrong.

**One set.** `indexBits` is 0, the index is always 0, and the mask
`(1 << 0) - 1` is `0` — which is exactly right, and only by accident if
you wrote the mask as a special case.

**One byte per block.** `offsetBits` is 0, so the offset is always 0 and
the index starts at bit 0. A cache like this has no spatial locality at
all: reading byte 5 does nothing for byte 6.

The trap underneath both is the shift. `1 << 64` on a 64-bit type is
**undefined behaviour**, not zero, so a mask written as
`(1ULL << bits) - 1` breaks for a 64-bit field. Here the fields are
small, but the habit of guarding the zero and full-width cases is the
one worth forming.

## Why a direct-mapped cache misses so much

The last three lines of the sample are the whole story. Addresses `0`
and `0x40` are 64 bytes apart, and the cache is 64 bytes, so they land
in the same set — and with one way, a set is one line. Alternating
between them misses every single time, however small the working set
is. That is a **conflict miss**, and it is the thing the next milestone
is about.
